extracted.intended_audience: aspiring courtiers, noblemen, and gentlemen seeking instruction in courtly deportment, speech, and writing (Renaissance-era etiquette and rhetorical training)
extracted.subtask_description: Instructions and standards for the perfect Courtier: bodily grace and nonchalance, imitation of masters, mastery of speech and writing, choice of diction, and the moral/behavioral virtues that make a courtier admired. Emphasizes both what to do and what to avoid (affectation, excess, poor imitation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Grace as universal seasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: The Courtier must accompany his actions, gestures, habits, in short his every movement, with grace; without grace other good qualities are of little worth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Grace is presented as a universal 'seasoning' that makes other virtues admirable; it should pervade everything the Courtier does.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grace: partly natural, partly acquirable
rubrics_metrics.description: Grace is oftentimes the gift of nature and of heaven, but when not perfect can, with care and pains, be made much greater.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Natural aptitude helps, but those with some capacity should pursue training and effort to increase grace; do not assume it's wholly innate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Begin early and learn fundamentals from the best masters
rubrics_metrics.description: Whoever would acquire grace in bodily exercises ought to begin early and learn the rudiments from the best masters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: King Philip chose Aristotle for Alexander; Galeazzo Sanseverino studied with proficient men like messer Pietro Monte. Practical implication: seek superior teachers and begin training young.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emulate masters but select the best from many
rubrics_metrics.description: A good pupil must put forth every effort to resemble his master and later observe different men of the same calling, selecting now this thing from one and that thing from another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogies: 'the bee' that robs flowers; warning against slavish imitation of a single trick (e.g., imitating a great man's single affectation). Transform virtues into one's own by combining the best parts of several models.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid affectation; practise nonchalance (sprezzatura)
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid affectation to the uttermost and practise a certain nonchalance that shall conceal design and show that what is done and said is done without effort and almost without thought.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Nonchalance (sprezzatura) should make art appear effortless; if the art is discovered it destroys credit. Anti-patterns: obvious striving, counting steps while dancing, forced poses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nonchalance must not be affected — avoid excess
rubrics_metrics.description: Nonchalance is praiseworthy in itself, but if it is exaggerated it becomes affectation and unbecoming; likewise excess in care of dress is offensive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of excess: letting cloak or slippers fall to prove 'not thinking about it', holding head stiff to protect hair, carrying a mirror in cap peak. Maintain moderation; both extremes offend.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conceal art — true art should not appear as art
rubrics_metrics.description: To be true art which does not appear to be art; we must give greater care to conceal art because its revelation destroys esteem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical example: ancient orators hiding learning to seem natural; practitioners should conceal their study so that seeming spontaneity impresses observers more than obvious labor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know when to stop — avoid over-diligence
rubrics_metrics.description: Over-diligence harms art; one must know when to take one's hand from the tablet (i.e., when a work is finished) to avoid affectation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anecdote: Apelles reproved Protogenes for not knowing when to finish. Anti-pattern: continuing beyond the point of finish makes work labored and ungraceful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Facility and ease reveal mastery
rubrics_metrics.description: A single easy, graceful movement or stroke, performed without strain, reveals the craftsman's knowledge and suggests he could do much more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples across disciplines: a poised posture with arms, a single graceful dance step, a musician ending with a sweet note, a painter's single unlaboured brush-stroke — all show excellence through apparent ease.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid ostentatious displays of learning or multilingualism
rubrics_metrics.description: Over-zeal to appear widely informed (e.g., suddenly speaking Roman, Spanish, or French) is an odious fault and an affectation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not use foreign words or affected speech merely to appear learned; such behaviour invites ridicule and undermines grace.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose diction appropriate to medium and audience
rubrics_metrics.description: What is proper in writing should be proper in speaking; writing is a form of speech and should use the most beautiful words used in speaking, but above all terms in use among the masses to ensure comprehension.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Debate noted: antique Tuscan words may add 'venerableness' in writing (Federico's view) but may be fatiguing or ridiculous in speech (Count's view). Practical rule: prefer words that communicate clearly in the given medium and audience, reserving obscure/antique terms for special effect sparingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Knowledge first — content precedes style
rubrics_metrics.description: What is chiefly important and necessary for the Courtier in order to speak and write well, is knowledge; an ignorant man cannot say or write anything that merits being heard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Style and graceful delivery are secondary; without substantial thought there is little to adorn. Emphasize learning and having something worthy to express.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arrange thoughts and use precise, choice language
rubrics_metrics.description: The Courtier must arrange in good order what he has to say or write; then express it well in words which ought to be precise, choice, rich and rightly formed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer words familiar in current use ('in use even among the masses') so that grandeur is communicated, and arrange words 'like pictures placed in good and proper light.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Speaking requires vocal quality, clear enunciation, and tempered gestures
rubrics_metrics.description: For speaking some things are required that are not needed in writing: a good voice (sonorous, clear, sweet, not thin nor rough), distinct enunciation, proper bearing and gestures tempered by a calm face and a play of the eyes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Movements should not be affected or violent; gestures should accord with words and express the speaker's intent and feeling as far as possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thoughts must be beautiful, ingenious, and suited to occasion
rubrics_metrics.description: The thoughts expressed by words must be beautiful, ingenious, acute, elegant and grave, according to the need.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Substance should match occasion: sometimes amusing and light, sometimes grave, and always lucid and elegant. Content quality determines the value of style and grace.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flexibility of register and rhetorical control
rubrics_metrics.description: The Courtier should speak of amusing things or grave matters as occasion demands, with readiness and lucid fullness; avoid vanity or childish folly; explain obscure subjects clearly and speak with dignity and force when needed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be adaptable: soften with 'simple candour' when desirable, kindle emotions forcefully when required, and make listeners feel the speaker attains excellence with little apparent effort.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use exemplary models (imitate the best) but do so judiciously
rubrics_metrics.description: Select as model someone who by consent of all is rated good and take him as a constant guide (Federico suggests Petrarch and Boccaccio); imitation is necessary to write well.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Imitate to learn, but avoid copying obsolete or inappropriate traits; combine lessons from multiple models and do not let imitation become mere affectation or habit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Occasional acceptance of foreign terms when understood
rubrics_metrics.description: Using some French or Spanish terms already accepted by custom may be permissible and even praiseworthy provided the Courtier hopes to be understood.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: terms like 'pritmor' (excellence) or 'un cavalier sensa riniproccio' (a cavalier without reproach) may be used sparingly for effect, but clarity is the priority.
